{{Short description|Type of singular integral operator}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] theory of [[harmonic analysis]], the '''Riesz transforms''' are a family of generalizations of the [[Hilbert transform]] to [[Euclidean space]]s of dimension ''d''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1.  They are a type of [[singular integral]] [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]], meaning that they are given by a [[convolution]] of one function with another function having a singularity at the origin.  Specifically, the Riesz transforms of a complex-valued function ƒ on '''R'''<sup>''d''</sup> are defined by
{{NumBlk|:|<math>R_jf(x) = c_d\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\int_{\mathbf{R}^d\backslash B_\epsilon(x)}\frac{(x_j-t_j)f(t)}{|x-t|^{d+1}}\,dt</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
for ''j''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,2,...,''d''.  The constant ''c''<sub>''d''</sub> is a dimensional normalization given by

:<math>c_d = \frac{1}{\pi\omega_{d-1}} = \frac{\Gamma[(d+1)/2]}{\pi^{(d+1)/2}}.</math>

where ω<sub>''d''&minus;1</sub> is the [[Volume of an n-ball|volume of the unit (''d''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)-ball]].  The limit is written in various ways, often as a [[Cauchy principal value|principal value]], or as a [[convolution]] with the [[distribution (mathematics)#Tempered distributions and Fourier transform|tempered distribution]]

:<math>K(x) = \frac{1}{\pi\omega_{d-1}} \, p.v. \frac{x_j}{|x|^{d+1}}.</math>

The Riesz transforms arises in the study of differentiability properties of harmonic potentials in [[potential theory]] and [[harmonic analysis]].  In particular, they arise in the proof of the Calderón-Zygmund inequality {{harv|Gilbarg|Trudinger|1983|loc=§9.4}}.

==Multiplier properties==

The Riesz transforms are given by a [[Fourier multiplier]].  Indeed, the [[Fourier transform]] of ''R''<sub>''j''</sub>ƒ is given by

:<math>\mathcal{F}(R_jf)(x) = -i\frac{x_j}{|x|}(\mathcal{F}f)(x).</math>

In this form, the Riesz transforms are seen to be generalizations of the [[Hilbert transform]].  The kernel is a [[distribution (mathematics)|distribution]] which is [[homogeneous function|homogeneous]] of degree zero.  A particular consequence of this last observation is that the Riesz transform defines a [[bounded linear operator]] from ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''d''</sup>) to itself.<ref>Strictly speaking, the definition ({{EquationNote|1}}) may only make sense for [[Schwartz function]] ''f''.  Boundedness on a dense subspace of ''L''<sup>2</sup> implies that each Riesz transform admits a continuous linear extension to all of ''L''<sup>2</sup>.</ref>

This homogeneity property can also be stated more directly without the aid of the Fourier transform. If σ<sub>''s''</sub> is the [[Homothetic transformation|dilation]] on '''R'''<sup>''d''</sup> by the scalar ''s'', that is σ<sub>''s''</sub>''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''sx'', then σ<sub>''s''</sub> defines an action on functions via [[pullback (differential geometry)|pullback]]:

:<math>\sigma_s^* f = f\circ\sigma_s.</math>

The Riesz transforms commute with σ<sub>''s''</sub>:

:<math>\sigma_s^* (R_jf) = R_j(\sigma_x^*f).</math>

Similarly, the Riesz transforms commute with translations.  Let τ<sub>''a''</sub> be the translation on '''R'''<sup>''d''</sup> along the vector ''a''; that is, τ<sub>''a''</sub>(''x'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''a''.  Then

:<math>\tau_a^* (R_jf) = R_j(\tau_a^*f).</math>

For the final property, it is convenient to regard the Riesz transforms as a single [[Vector (geometric)|vectorial]] entity ''R''ƒ&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''R''<sub>1</sub>ƒ,...,''R''<sub>''d''</sub>ƒ).  Consider a [[rotation]] ρ in '''R'''<sup>''d''</sup>.  The rotation acts on spatial variables, and thus on functions via pullback.  But it also can act on the spatial vector ''R''ƒ.  The final transformation property asserts that the Riesz transform is [[equivariant]] with respect to these two actions; that is,

:<math>\rho^* R_j [(\rho^{-1})^*f] = \sum_{k=1}^d \rho_{jk} R_kf.</math>

These three properties in fact characterize the Riesz transform in the following sense.  Let ''T''=(''T''<sub>''1''</sub>,...,''T''<sub>''d''</sub>) be a ''d''-tuple of bounded linear operators from ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''d''</sup>) to ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''d''</sup>) such that

* ''T'' commutes with all dilations and translations.
* ''T'' is equivariant with respect to rotations.

Then, for some constant ''c'', ''T'' = ''cR''.

==Relationship with the Laplacian==
Formally, the Riesz transforms can be identified with [[Fractional derivative|fractional derivatives]] via

<math>R f = -\,\nabla (-\Delta)^{-1/2} f</math>, 

that is, <math>R_j = -\,\partial_j (-\Delta)^{-1/2}</math>. 

In particular, one has the operator identity

<math>\partial_i \partial_j = -\,R_i R_j \Delta</math>,

valid as Fourier multipliers on <math>\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^d)</math> and, by extension, on the space of [[tempered distributions]] <math>\mathcal{S}'</math>. 

For [[Schwartz space|Schwartz functions]] <math>u</math>, this implies

<math>R_i R_j(\Delta u) = -\,\tfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}</math>. 

The situation becomes subtler for general tempered distributions. If <math>\Delta u \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)</math>, then <math>u</math> is determined modulo [[Affine transformation|affine functions]], which have vanishing second derivatives, and the above identity holds in <math>L^2</math> without correction. 

More generally, if <math>u</math> is such that <math>\Delta u</math> has only tempered growth but not integrability (for instance, if <math>u</math> is a quadratic polynomial), then additional polynomial terms may appear:

<math>\tfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}
= -\,R_i R_j (\Delta u) + P_{ij}(x)</math>,

where <math>P_{ij}</math> is a polynomial depending on <math>u</math>. This reflects the fact that inversion of the Laplacian is only well-defined on tempered distributions modulo polynomials.
